[{"title":"Business Growth Without Culture: Lessons from Uber","category":"","date":"","read":"","author":"","image":"/content/media/1793073260677_People__Leadership__Culture__Growth.webp","excerpt":"","content":"Can a Company Grow Bigger While Becoming Weaker From Within?

Imagine building a company from a bold idea into a global business. Your customer base is expanding. Your team is growing. New markets are opening up. Your brand is becoming increasingly recognized. From the outside, everything looks successful. But inside the organization, something is changing.
Employees hesitate to speak openly. Managers begin prioritizing targets over people. Different teams develop conflicting ways of working. Behaviour that once would have been unacceptable gradually becomes tolerated because the people displaying it deliver results.
The company continues to grow, but the experience of working there begins to change. Customers may still recognize the brand. Revenue may still increase. The business may continue entering new markets. Yet the organization risks losing something fundamental: the culture that enables people to work together, trust one another and build something meaningful.
This is not merely a hypothetical situation. The experience of Uber offers a powerful real-world lesson about what can happen when organizational culture, leadership and accountability fail to develop alongside business ambitions.

The Rise of Uber: An Ambition to Transform an Industry

     Uber began in 2009 with an ambitious idea: use technology to transform how people travel. The company challenged established transportation models and expanded rapidly across cities and countries. Its willingness to question conventional approaches helped it become one of the most prominent technology businesses in the world.
     Its story demonstrated the power of ambition, innovation and execution. But business success introduced another challenge. As organizations expand, their leaders can no longer personally influence every interaction, decision and behaviour. The business becomes more complex. New employees join. Managers take responsibility for teams. Performance expectations influence everyday decisions.
     The founder's original vision must now travel through layers of leadership, systems and processes. This is where culture becomes critically important. A company cannot depend indefinitely on the founder being present to explain what matters. It must build a shared understanding of how people are expected to work, make decisions and treat one another.
Uber's subsequent experience demonstrated what can happen when serious cultural problems emerge within a rapidly growing organization.

The Turning Point: When an Employee Spoke Up

     In February 2017, former Uber engineer Susan Fowler published an account of her experience working at the company. She described alleged sexual harassment, difficulties in getting her complaints addressed and concerns about how management handled the situation. Her account attracted widespread attention and prompted questions about the company's workplace environment and the systems intended to protect employees.

     Uber commissioned an independent investigation led by former US Attorney General Eric Holder and his colleague Tammy Albarrán. The investigation resulted in recommendations concerning leadership, workplace practices, employee complaints, governance and organizational culture.
     
     The issue was no longer simply about individual incidents. It had become a broader question about leadership accountability and the environment in which people worked. In June 2017, Uber's board adopted the investigation's recommendations. The company was being forced to confront a difficult question: What happens when the behaviours an organization tolerates contradict the values it claims to uphold?

The Deeper Lesson: Your Real Culture Is Revealed by Your Decisions

     One of the most important lessons from Uber's experience concerns the relationship between stated values and actual behaviour. An organization might say that it values respect, integrity, teamwork and accountability. But employees do not experience values merely by reading them on a wall or in an employee handbook.

They experience them through everyday decisions. 
•	What happens when a high-performing manager behaves inappropriately? 
•	What happens when an employee raises a concern about a senior colleague? 
•	What happens when a team misses its targets? 
•	What happens when delivering results conflicts with treating people fairly?

     The answers to these questions reveal the culture people actually experience. Uber's investigation highlighted how certain cultural slogans, including "Always Be Hustling’" and "Let Builders Build," could be used to justify inappropriate behaviour.
     The lesson is not that ambition; speed or ownership are undesirable. These qualities can be essential to business success. The problem arises when they are interpreted without clear boundaries or when accountability becomes inconsistent.
Consider the difference:
•	Ambition without responsibility can encourage people to pursue results at the expense of others.
•	Speed without judgment can encourage shortcuts that create long-term problems.
•	Performance without accountability can allow high-performing individuals to escape standards that apply to everyone else.
•	Ownership without respect can turn initiative into behaviour that damages collaboration.

     A value is useful only when people understand what it means in practice and the organization consistently supports it. Culture is not simply what a company says it believes. It is what its people learn to do, accept and repeat.

The Hidden Risk: Growth Multiplies the Impact of Leadership

     When a business is small, the founder can often resolve problems personally. The founder knows the employees, speaks directly with customers, understands operational challenges and can intervene when something goes wrong.
But growth changes the equation. A company with ten employees operates differently from one with one hundred. A company with one hundred employees operates differently from one with one thousand. Communication becomes more complex.           Decisions move through managers. Employees experience the organization through different departments and leaders.
Even when the founder's intentions remain unchanged, employees may experience very different cultures across the organization. One manager may encourage open communication, while another discourages disagreement. One department may prioritize customer satisfaction, while another focuses exclusively on internal targets. One leader may take responsibility for mistakes, while another looks for someone to blame.
Over time, these differences influence how people behave and what they believe the organization truly values. This is why culture cannot be left entirely to chance. The larger the organization becomes, the more deliberately its culture must be developed. Growth requires more than additional people, facilities, technology and processes. It requires leadership practices and systems that help the organization maintain a shared sense of purpose.
What Happened Next? The Challenge of Rebuilding Trust
Uber's response provides another important lesson. Following the investigation, the company adopted recommendations intended to strengthen oversight, accountability and workplace practices. It also began changing its cultural values.
In November 2017, Uber introduced revised cultural norms that emphasized principles including doing the right thing, acting like owners, celebrating differences and valuing ideas over hierarchy.
These changes reflected a recognition that culture needed attention beyond slogans and statements. Changing a culture, however, is not as simple as changing a document.
Employees need to see that leaders demonstrate the stated values. Managers need to understand how those values should influence decisions. Systems need to support the expected behaviours. People need to know that concerns will be taken seriously.
Otherwise, the new language may change while the old experience remains. Uber's experience does not establish that every cultural problem can be eliminated through a new set of values. Nor does it prove that its later reforms resolved every challenge.
It demonstrates something more fundamental: when an organization's culture becomes a serious concern, rebuilding trust requires deliberate attention to leadership, systems and behaviour. The work must continue long after the announcement of new values.
Five Lessons for Business Owners
Uber's experience offers valuable lessons for any organization that wants to grow without compromising the quality of its working environment.

1. Define What Success Really Means

Business success is often measured through revenue, profitability, market share, productivity and growth. These measures matter. But they do not tell the complete story of an organization.
Consider asking:
•	Are our customers genuinely benefiting from working with us?
•	Are our employees developing and becoming more capable?
•	Do our people feel comfortable raising concerns?
•	Do our vendors and partners trust us to honour our commitments?
•	Are our leaders proud of how results are being achieved?
A business can achieve short-term targets while creating long-term problems that are not immediately visible in its financial reports. Sustainable success requires attention to both business results and the way those results are achieved.

2. Translate Values Into Observable Behaviours

Words such as integrity, ownership, teamwork and respect can mean different things to different people. For one manager, ownership may mean solving problems independently. For another, it may mean taking decisions without consulting anyone. Without shared expectations, employees may interpret the same value in conflicting ways. Organizations should define what their values look like in everyday work. For example:
Value: Ownership
Observable behaviours:
•	Take responsibility for commitments.
•	Communicate risks before they become major problems.
•	Acknowledge mistakes and help resolve them.
•	Focus on solutions rather than blame.
Value: Respect
Observable behaviours:
•	Listen to others without dismissing their concerns.
•	Give feedback without humiliation.
•	Treat people fairly regardless of position.
•	Address inappropriate behaviour consistently.

When values become observable behaviours, employees have a clearer understanding of what is expected. Culture becomes something they can practise rather than something they are merely asked to believe in.

3. Never Allow Performance to Replace Accountability

One of the most damaging messages an organization can send is that exceptional performance excuses unacceptable behaviour. Imagine a sales manager who consistently achieves targets but repeatedly disrespects colleagues. If leadership ignores the behaviour because the manager produces strong results, other employees receive a message.
They may conclude that respect is optional for high performers. Similarly, if a senior leader ignores agreed procedures but continues to be rewarded, employees may conclude that accountability applies only to people with less power.
Over time, such inconsistencies undermine trust. A healthy organization recognizes both what people achieve and how they achieve it. Performance matters. So do integrity, collaboration, responsibility and respect. These should reinforce one another rather than compete for attention.

4. Develop Leaders Who Can Carry the Culture Forward

The founder's personal example is powerful, particularly in the early stages of a business. But sustainable growth requires more leaders who understand and demonstrate the organization's values.
Managers are not simply responsible for achieving departmental targets. They also shape the environment in which people work. They influence whether employees feel safe to ask questions, whether mistakes become opportunities to learn, whether conflicts are resolved constructively and whether people take responsibility for their commitments.
As a business expands, developing these leadership capabilities becomes increasingly important. The goal is not to make every manager behave identically. It is to create consistency in the principles that guide their decisions. A strong culture allows different people to lead in their own ways while remaining aligned with the organization's purpose and standards.
5. Review Culture as Deliberately as You Review Business Performance
Most businesses review financial results, sales pipelines, production performance and operational efficiency. But how often do they systematically examine the behaviours producing those results? Culture should not be evaluated only when a serious problem emerges. Business leaders can regularly examine:
•	Whether employees understand the company's values.
•	Whether managers consistently demonstrate those values.
•	Whether incentives encourage the right behaviours.
•	Whether employees can raise concerns without fear of unfair treatment.
•	Whether customers receive the experience the organization promises.
•	Whether teams collaborate effectively across departments.
Employee feedback, customer feedback, leadership reviews and observations of everyday work can help identify gaps between the intended culture and the experienced culture. The objective is not to measure culture for its own sake. It is to identify where the organization can improve how people work together and how those improvements can support business performance.
Culture Is Not an HR Project. It Is a Business Responsibility.

Culture is sometimes treated as the responsibility of the human resources department. HR may coordinate policies, employee feedback, training and development initiatives. But culture is shaped by decisions throughout the organization.
•	The sales department influences culture through the targets it pursues and the promises it makes to customers. 
•	Operations influences culture through its approach to quality, safety and problem-solving.
•	Finance influences culture through the controls it establishes and the behaviours it rewards. 
•	Managers influence culture through how they communicate, delegate, resolve conflicts and hold people accountable. 
•	The founder influences culture through what they prioritize, what they tolerate and how they respond when difficult decisions must be made.

This is why culture must be connected to the way the business actually operates. A workshop can introduce values. A presentation can explain expectations. A policy can define standards. But lasting change requires these principles to become part of everyday decisions, management practices and organizational systems.
The real test of culture is what happens when leaders are not in the room.
Do people still take responsibility?
Do they still treat customers fairly?
Do they still support their colleagues?
Do they still make decisions consistent with the organization's values?
The answers reveal whether culture has become part of the organization's way of working.
The Bigger Opportunity: Build an Organization Where Everyone Can Grow
The purpose of developing culture should not be limited to preventing problems. It should also help create a better organization. 
•	Imagine a business where customers feel confident about the promises being made to them.
•	Employees feel that their contributions matter and that they have opportunities to develop. 
•	Managers take responsibility for results while supporting the people who produce them. 
•	Vendors and partners are treated fairly and can trust the organization to honour its commitments. 
•	And the founder feels proud not only of the company's growth but also of the way it operates.
Such an organization is pursuing more than expansion. It is building a system in which business success and human development can reinforce one another. This does not mean avoiding difficult decisions or compromising performance expectations. It means pursuing ambitious goals while remaining clear about the principles that guide the journey.
A strong culture does not eliminate every disagreement, mistake or challenge. It helps people navigate those challenges with greater clarity, responsibility and mutual respect. That is what makes culture an important part of sustainable business transformation.
Final reflection: as your company grows, what must grow with it?
Uber's experience reminds us that a successful business can face serious cultural challenges when leadership, workplace practices and accountability do not adequately support the environment an organization needs.
The lesson is not to choose between growth and culture. It is to recognize that business growth creates a responsibility to develop the organization that supports it. More employees require stronger leadership. More managers require clearer expectations. More complex operations require better communication and accountability. And greater ambition requires a shared understanding of how success should be achieved.
A company's culture should not remain frozen in the past. It must evolve as the organization grows while preserving the principles that make the business worth building. Because the ultimate goal is not simply to create a bigger organization. It is to create an organization that becomes more capable, more responsible and more valuable to the people associated with it as it grows.
At Nucleus Consultant, we believe that sustainable business transformation is about more than improving business performance. It is about building organizations where business growth, leadership development and human growth move forward together.
So, if you are leading a growing business, consider one important question:
As your company grows bigger, are you deliberately building a culture that makes it better for your customers, your employees, your partners and yourself?
